ALMA Cycle-2 observations in the millimeter continuum (∼0′′.25 angular resolution) show that the disk is elongated with an apparent asymmetry (Cieza et al. 2018), indicating the presence of an unresolved structure or a secondary disk.
Here, we present follow-up observations at ∼0′′.03, resolving the system into two components: HBC 494 N (primary) and HBC 494 S (secondary). No circumbinary disk was detected.
The observations show that the primary is ∼5 times brighter/more massive and ∼2 times bigger than the secondary.
We notice that the northern component has a similar mass to the FUors, while the southern has to EXors. The HBC 494 disks show individual sizes that are smaller than single eruptive YSOs.

A clear difference is seen when we compare the disks from multiple systems (hexagon symbols) and single systems. The latter present bigger sizes as they are not targets for tidal truncation, enhanced radial drift, and more aggressive photoevaporation
The HBC 494 disks have similar inclinations (Δ𝑖 = 7.5 ± 4.1 degrees) and similar PAs (Δ𝑃𝐴 = 4.6 ± 7.0 degrees). The relative orientations of the disks suggest that the system is coplanar.

Thus, we tentatively suggest that HBC 494 was formed by rotational disk fragmentation rather than direct collapsing. However, more precise observation of the kinematics of the surrounding gas on a small scale (Vorobyov et al. 2021), complemented with orbital information coming from astrometrical measurements, is required to evaluate this hypothesis.

At a smaller scale, the 12CO and 13CO moment zero maps show cavities within the continuum disks’ area, which may indicate continuum over-subtraction or slow-moving jets and chemical destruction along the line-of-sight.

The disk sizes were calculated using the deconvolved Gaussian FWHM/2 radius obtained from 2D Gaussian fits. This methodology was also used for other ALMA datasets (e.g., Hales et al. 2020; Tobin et al. 2020). Therefore, it allows a consistent comparison with other disks.

For each HBC 494 disk, no clue of trigger mechanisms was found, since the gas and continuum data did not reveal clear spiral or clumpy features indicating a case of infall or GI (see e.g., Zhu et al. 2012; Kratter & Lodato 2016).

Looking at the dust continuum (Figure 2), CO isotopologues moment maps (Figure 7), and the scattered 12CO emission (Figure 12 of Ruíz-Rodríguez et al. 2017), the hypothesis of stellar flybys is also not encouraged since no trace of perturbation was detected (Cuello et al. 2020, 2023).
